A simple exponential population-growth model assumes that the per-capita growth rate remains constant. If observations showed a population growing more slowly than the model predicts, students could question the conditions it leaves out, including changes in resources or other influences on birth and death rates. They might then revise the model or specify when its assumptions remain useful. Deciding what would count as an adequate explanation could become part of their investigation.

-

Students may be able to critique scientific models without having the same influence over the criteria used to judge them. In a fifth-grade inquiry, written reflection on peer critiques and class discussion supported students in revising their class's criteria (Murphy et al., 2023). In a seventh-grade study, students used visual, verbal, and written resources to evaluate and revise models against criteria selected in advance by the researchers and teachers (Cheung & Yang, 2026).

-

A learning progression for scientific modelling describes how students may come to treat models as tools for explaining and predicting, as well as representations that can change with new understanding (Schwarz et al., 2009). The questions students are trying to resolve also shape how scientific practices and argumentation become meaningful (Berland et al., 2016; Manz, 2015).

+

A simple population-growth model might predict continued increase while assuming that reproduction remains relatively stable and resources do not constrain growth. Observations of a slowing population would give students grounds to question those assumptions. They could examine which relationships the model represents, what it leaves out, and whether revising it would help explain the observed pattern. The decision about what makes a model adequate can itself become part of the inquiry.

+

Students can evaluate scientific models while having different degrees of influence over what counts as a good model. In a fifth-grade inquiry, written reflection on peer critiques and class discussion supported students in revising their class's criteria (Murphy et al., 2023). In a seventh-grade study, students used visual, verbal, and written resources to evaluate and revise models against criteria selected in advance by the researchers and teachers (Cheung & Yang, 2026).

+

A learning progression for scientific modelling describes how students may come to treat models as tools for explaining and predicting, as well as representations that can change with new understanding (Schwarz et al., 2009). Studies of scientific practices and argumentation further locate students' explanations within the problems they are trying to resolve (Berland et al., 2016; Manz, 2015). I am interested in what happens when students are invited to question the adequacy of an established classroom model and whether their judgments can influence the scientific work that follows.
